nameStory: Despite its name, the Bald Eagle isn't actually bald! The name comes from an old English word 'balde' meaning white-headed, referring to the striking white feathers that crown an adult's head. Early European settlers used this older meaning of 'bald' to describe the bird's distinctive white head feathers contrasting against its dark brown body.
description: The Bald Eagle is North America's most iconic bird of prey and our national bird. Adults are unmistakable with their gleaming white heads and tails contrasting sharply against chocolate-brown bodies and wings. These powerful raptors are massive birds, with females growing about 25% larger than males, and they build the largest nests of any North American bird. Young eagles look completely different - they're mottled brown all over and don't develop their famous white head and tail until they're 4-5 years old.

idTips.label: White head and tail
idTips.description: Adult birds have brilliant white head and tail feathers that almost seem to glow against their dark brown body - like they're wearing a white cap and have been dipped in white paint from the tail up

idTips.label: Massive yellow beak
idTips.description: The beak is bright yellow-orange and powerfully hooked, looking almost too large for the head - about the size of your thumb and designed for tearing fish apart

idTips.label: Enormous size
idTips.description: Even at a distance, these birds look huge with wings that span wider than a person is tall - when soaring, they dwarf other large birds like Red-tailed Hawks

idTips.label: Flat-winged soaring
idTips.description: In flight, they hold their wings perfectly flat and straight out from their body like a board, never tilted upward in a 'V' shape like Turkey Vultures

idTips.label: Juveniles are mottled brown
idTips.description: Young birds under 5 years old are splotchy brown and white all over with no distinct white head or tail - they look like a completely different species

habitat: Look for Bald Eagles near large bodies of water throughout New England - major rivers, lakes, reservoirs, and coastal areas where fish are abundant. They prefer areas with tall, sturdy old-growth trees nearby for nesting, especially white pines and oaks that can support their massive stick nests. You'll often spot them perched on dead snags overlooking the water or soaring high above wetlands and waterways.

seasonality.spring: Eagles are busy building or renovating their enormous stick nests and beginning to raise young. Look for pairs carrying large branches to nest sites in tall trees near water.
seasonality.summer: Adults are feeding hungry nestlings and teaching recently fledged young to hunt. You might see family groups near water with mottled-brown juveniles begging for food from white-headed parents.
seasonality.fall: Migration brings northern eagles through New England, and you may see multiple eagles fishing in the same area. Young birds are learning to hunt independently and can be quite vocal.
seasonality.winter: Eagles concentrate near unfrozen water sources and fish runs. This is often the best time for viewing as they're more predictable in their feeding locations and easier to spot against snowy landscapes.

funFact: Bald Eagle nests can weigh as much as a small car - up to 2,000 pounds! The largest recorded nest was 13 feet deep and 8 feet wide, and eagles keep adding to the same nest year after year until the tree literally can't support it anymore and crashes down.
confusionNotes: Young Bald Eagles are often confused with Golden Eagles or even large hawks because they lack the white head and tail. Remember: if it's near water and absolutely massive with a huge yellow beak, it's probably a young Bald Eagle. Golden Eagles prefer mountains and have smaller, darker beaks.
contextualKnowledge: Bald Eagles are one of America's greatest conservation success stories - they were nearly extinct in the lower 48 states by the 1970s due to DDT poisoning, but have made a remarkable comeback after the pesticide was banned. Seeing one in New England today represents decades of dedicated conservation work and the resilience of nature.
compareHints: The only other sea-eagle you might encounter is Steller's Sea-Eagle, but that's an extremely rare vagrant from Alaska with an even more massive yellow beak and more white markings. Within the hawk family, Bald Eagles are much larger than any other raptor in New England, with that distinctive flat-winged soaring posture and preference for waterside habitats that sets them apart from forest-dwelling hawks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Bald Eagle, Steller's Sea Eagle is significantly larger and bulkier with a much more massive beak.
